en: The *Buddha-bhāṣita-manas-sūtra*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Anāthapiṇḍada Park.
In the Jeta Grove,
at that time, a certain bhikṣu was sitting alone in his cell, and this thought arose in his mind:
"For what reason is the world dragged along?"
"For what reason does one experience suffering?
For what reason, having been born again and again, does one enter into its succession?
Then that bhikṣu rose from his seat in the late afternoon; having risen, he went to where the Blessed One was, and upon arrival, he prostrated at the Blessed One’s feet and sat down to one side.
Having sat down to one side, that bhikṣu addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"Venerable Sir! Today, while I was alone in my cell, this thought arose in my mind: [text continues]"
"For what reason is the world dragged along?
For what reason does it undergo suffering?
For what reason, having been born again and again, does it enter into its subsequent course?"
"Excellent, excellent, bhikṣu! You possess a noble path, a noble contemplation, and skillful eloquence; what you have reflected upon is excellent."
"For what reason is the world dragged along?
For what reason does it undergo suffering?
For what reason, having been born again and again, does it enter into its subsequent course?"
"Did you, bhikṣu, ask such a question? "Indeed, World-Honored One, I did."
“Monks! It is because of the mind that the world is dragged along; it is because of the mind that one undergoes suffering. Having generated the mind, the mind follows after it. Monks!”
Yet it causes the world to be dragged along, to undergo suffering, and to follow after what has been born and what continues to be born.
Bhikkhus! The noble disciple is unattached; he is not dragged by that, does not go away because of that, and does not follow after what has been born and what continues to be born.
"Monks! A noble disciple who is an Arhat is able to govern his own mind; he does not let his mind follow its own whims.
"Excellent, World-Honored One!"
Having heard what the World-Honored One had said, that bhikṣu rejoiced and approved with delight, and he questioned the World-Honored One again, saying:
"World-Honored One! Regarding the 'bhikṣu who is learned,' regarding the 'bhikṣu who is learned'—World-Honored One!"
"By what measure is one called a 'bhikṣu of great learning,' and how many kinds of bhikṣus of great learning has the Tathāgata described? "Excellent, excellent!"
"Monks! This is the noble path, the noble contemplation, and the eloquence; what has been said is excellent.
'World-Honored One!'"
"O World-Honored One! Regarding the 'bhikṣu who is much-heard' (bahuśruta), by how many qualities is one called a bhikṣu who is much-heard?
How many things does the Tathāgata say constitute a bhikṣu who is much-heard?"
“Did you, bhikṣu, ask such a question? “Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”

“I have frequently spoken of twelve types of discourses for bhikṣus: first, the sūtras; second, the geyas; third, the vyākaraṇas; fourth, the gāthās; fifth, the nidānas; sixth, the dharmapadas; seventh, the avadānas; eighth, the upadeśas; ninth, the jātaka; tenth, the vaipulya; eleventh, the adbhutadharmas; and twelfth, the upadeśas.”

If a son of good family among the bhikṣus were to recite even a four-line verse to me, he would know its meaning and know the Dharma; his practice would accord with the Dharma, he would be fully endowed with the Dharma, and his conduct and speech would be in accordance with the Dharma.
"In this way, a bhikṣu is one who has heard much; in this way, a bhikṣu is considered one who has heard much; in this way, the Tathāgata describes a bhikṣu as one who has heard much.
"Excellent, World-Honored One!"
Having heard what the World-Honored One had said, that bhikṣu reflected upon it well, took delight in it, and approved of it; he then asked the World-Honored One again:
"World-Honored One!..."
Having heard this, the bhikṣu asked: "Having heard this, the bhikṣu possesses swift wisdom.
World-Honored One, in what sense is it said that a bhikṣu has 'heard' and is said to possess 'swift wisdom'?"
“The Tathāgata has spoken of how many bhikṣus have attained swift and rapid wisdom upon hearing it? “Excellent,
excellent, bhikṣu!”
"Virtuous conduct, virtuous contemplation, and eloquence—your words are excellent.
'Indeed, World-Honored One!
Once a bhikṣu has heard this, a bhikṣu who has heard it possesses swift and keen wisdom.'"
“World-Honored One!
How many bhikṣus have you said possess swift and sharp wisdom after hearing [the Dharma]? “Did you, bhikṣu, ask this?”
“Yes, indeed, World-Honored One! “Monk!

When that monk has heard about suffering, he knows it as it truly is through wisdom; he knows the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the way leading to the cessation of suffering. This is what is meant by having heard [the teaching], and knowing it as it truly is through wisdom: the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the way leading to the cessation of suffering. This is what is meant by having heard [the teaching], and knowing it as it truly is through wisdom.”
"In this way, bhikṣus!
That bhikṣu, having heard it, possesses swift wisdom; thus, the Tathāgata says that a bhikṣu, having heard it in this way, possesses swift wisdom.
"Excellent, World-Honored One!"
Having heard what the Blessed One had said, that bhikṣu was well-pleased and approved it; he then asked the Blessed One again: "O Blessed One!
A bhikṣu who possesses clever eloquence and quick wit—O Blessed One! a bhikṣu who possesses clever wisdom and quick wit—"
"How many are called bhikṣus who possess intelligence, wisdom, and swift eloquence?
How many bhikṣus does the Tathāgata describe as possessing intelligence, wisdom, and swift eloquence? "Excellent, excellent!"
"Monks! The noble path, noble contemplation, and eloquence—what you have said is excellent.
'Indeed, World-Honored One!'"
"Bhagavān, regarding a bhikṣu who is clever, wise, and quick-witted— a bhikṣu who is clever, eloquent, and quick-witted—
how much must he possess for the Blessed One to say that he is a bhikṣu who is clever, wise, and quick-witted?"
“How many bhikṣus does the Tathāgata say possess intelligence, wisdom, and swift eloquence?
“Did you ask this, bhikṣu? “Indeed, World-Honored One.”

"O Bhikṣu! This means that a bhikṣu does not think of himself, does not think of others, and does not think of both; having stilled his mind, the bhikṣu brings benefit to himself and benefit to others, benefiting many people out of compassion for the world, and through this righteous purpose, he benefits devas and humans."
"In this way, a bhikṣu is intelligent, wise, and swift; the Tathāgata says that such a bhikṣu is intelligent, eloquent, and swift in wisdom.
"Excellent, World-Honored One!"

Having heard what the Blessed One had said, that bhikṣu reflected upon it well, took it to heart, and recited it; then he rose from his seat, prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated the Blessed One, and departed from the Blessed One’s presence.
The Blessed One spoke this parable for their sake: "Dwelling alone in seclusion, with an undistracted mind, one abides in tranquility.

Having dwelt alone in seclusion with an undistracted mind in tranquility—O son of noble family, he who has shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and out of faith and joy has gone forth from the household life to study the Way—he practices the unsurpassed holy life, realizes the Dharma through direct knowledge, attains the fruits of realization, and dwells therein, knowing according to reality: 'Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and for name-and-form there is no further existence.'"
That venerable one had already realized the Dharma and attained the state of an Arhat.
Thus spoke the Buddha; having heard what the World-Honored One said, that bhikṣu rejoiced and was glad.
The Sūtra on the Mind Spoken by the Buddha
